title: Reading drawings and schematics
hook: You lock off the breaker that feeds a pump on its single-line diagram, yet the pump's starter is still live. The drawing is right. What did you miss on it?
oneBreath: Every system diagram, electrical, hydraulic, air or pipework, is a map of what is joined to what, not a picture of the plant. Find the sources, find the state it is drawn in, then trace one path at a time, and the four kinds become one skill with four sets of symbols. An engineering drawing is the odd one out: it shows one object's shape, seen square-on from several sides and set out by a fixed rule.

ideas.title: How any diagram talks
ideas.oneLine: Any system diagram maps what is joined to what, not where parts sit, so you read it by following connections, never by layout.

ideas.title: Single-line diagrams: from each source to each load
ideas.oneLine: Trace a single-line diagram, a board's power map, from each source to each load, seeing what every breaker feeds and which loads have two feeds.

ideas.title: Control schematics: coils, contacts and cross-references
ideas.oneLine: A control schematic draws each contact apart from the coil that moves it; the cross-reference under each coil finds its contacts, wherever they are drawn.

ideas.title: Fluid power symbols
ideas.oneLine: Hydraulic and air symbols are built from simple marks that each mean one thing, so you can read one you have never met.

ideas.title: Valves in fluid power
ideas.oneLine: A valve that steers oil or air is drawn as one box per position, and only the box against the ports shows where it flows.

ideas.title: Tracing a hydraulic circuit, then a pneumatic one
ideas.oneLine: For each valve position, trace the supply to one side of a cylinder, and the other side out to the tank or, in air, the exhaust.

ideas.title: Piping and system diagrams
ideas.oneLine: On a piping diagram, flow runs only along open paths from a running pump, so you can find which valves to shut to isolate a part.

ideas.title: Engineering drawings
ideas.oneLine: An engineering drawing shows one object in several square-on views, laid out by a fixed rule, so you can rebuild its shape in your head.

ideas.title: Reading one you have never seen
ideas.oneLine: Read a diagram you have never seen in four steps: legend, sources, the state it is drawn in, then one path at a time.

calibration.q: On a circuit drawing, two wires cross in the middle of the page with no dot where they meet. Are they joined?
options: Yes, wires that touch on paper are joined
No, they just pass over each other
It depends where they sit in the real panel
calibration.why: On circuit drawings a crossing with no dot is two wires passing over each other, and a dot is drawn where wires join. Lines touching on paper is not a join, and where the wires sit in the panel does not change what the drawing joins.

calibration.q: Two pumps are wired so only one runs at once. A switch in pump B's circuit opens whenever A runs. On the drawing, is it shown open or closed?
options: Open, because A runs most of the time
Either, whichever way the drawer chose
Closed, as it sits with everything switched off
calibration.why: Control drawings show every switch as it sits with nothing switched on, so this one is drawn closed, even though it is open whenever A runs. A drawing that followed what usually happens would need redrawing each time the plant changed.
